subject: [PATCH v5 01/11] mm, swap: add virtual swap device infrastructure

reviews.author: Chris Li
reviews.summary:
Reviewer Chris Li expressed disagreement with making vswap a special device, citing the need for xswap to be treated as a normal swap device to avoid issues like lock ordering violations and per-CPU allocation caching problems.

Reviewer Chris Li acknowledged the patch's design choice as a careful one, but noted that it usually comes with both pros and cons, indicating a neutral sentiment.

Reviewer Chris Li questioned the patch's approach to handling uncompressible pages in xswap, suggesting that xswap could store them within itself instead of rejecting them, and noted a similarity with zswap's behavior.

Reviewer Chris Li noted that xswap doesn't require a lower tier and should not need to check for swap_is_xswap(), as it lacks the baggage associated with zswap's writeback enable interface.

Reviewer Chris Li noted that the issue of swap tiering and priority is not specific to vswap, but rather a problem area in the core swap layer, which will be addressed by a separate series.

Reviewer Chris Li suggests using Baoquan's writeback series as a base for the patch, citing it as being closer to his intended design and a more suitable foundation for further development.

Reviewer Chris Li expressed disappointment that the original author did not follow his suggestion to use a proper swap_ops approach, which would eliminate the need for most of the swap_is_vswap() checks.

Reviewer Chris Li expressed concerns that the vswap patch will break existing /etc/fstab configurations, including support for UUIDs, and change user-visible behavior by enabling vswap without explicit user action. He suggested adopting a design philosophy similar to VFS-like file systems for swap, where each swap device has its own superblock.

Reviewer Chris Li expressed strong disagreement with the patch series, citing that it is 'unclean' due to excessive special cases and requested a more general solution.
reviews.raw_body:
Ack, that is why I am against making it a special device. That is the
whole idea behind xswap. It is just normal swap device implemented via
swap_ops just like ext4 is a file system implemnet on top of VFS.

---

That is a careful design choice. Keep in mind that design choice
usually has pros and cons.

I will follow your feedback here.

---

I am not sure I follow. Are you referring to the uncompressible pages
that xswap would have to reject?

One way to address that is for xswap to just bite the bullet and store
the uncompressible pages within xswap. That way it will stay out of
the reclaim LRU. Zswap also stores some uncompressible pages. The last
time I checked, it was unfortunately not able to serve my case but
perfect for yours.

---

If xswap needs the lower tier it can allocate for one. I don't think
xswap should need to have swap_is_xswap() there. Also xswap does not
have all the baggage of zswap.writeback enable interface.

---

This will be addressed by the swap tiers series if it is not delayed.
This should be addressed in the core swap layer not vswap. Kairui also
has some ideas to improve that. Yes, it is a problem area, but it is
not specific to xswap. We are well aware of it and have plans to
improve it.

---

Baoquan's writeback series is out. It is by no means perfect. But it
is much closer to what I have in mind. That is a much better base to
work on.

---

Yes, I already read your code I decide that most of the
swap_is_vswap() should not be needed if taking a proper swap_ops
approach. I wanted to offer you the chance to work closely with me to
achieve that, but you did not follow that suggestion.

Quote from my old email:
https://lore.kernel.org/all/CACePvbX+3tO91BmRwaLqf3Xia32GCemt3W8tayErG81BYLgrzA@mail.gmail.com/

"I am happy to spend some time working with you to discuss the generic
adopted version of vswap, if you are open to it. Or if you don't want
to waste time on it. I can have someone else or myself come up with
the generic adopted version of vswap for you to review, which I prefer
less."

Anyway, Baoquan's xswap writeback patch series is out. I suggest
following and improving that series instead.

---

I like universal interfaces. Your vswap will break the /etc/fstab. The
current suggestion for xswap using sysfs will break that as well.
I would like to keep the /etc/fstab interface working, including
support for UUIDs for swap devices, etc.
I am very concerned that vswap will start kicking in without me
explicitly enabling it. That changes the previous user-visible
behavior. It breaks my mental model. Please take this feedback
seriously.

It is a different design philosophy to adopt a swap device to
implement VFS-like file systems for swap, making them swap file
systems.
Just like all file systems have a superblock so you can probe what
file system it is. You don't get a special sysfs interface for each
different file system to create them.
This aligns neatly with swap ops and makes room for future
flash-friendly swap file systems for example.

---

That is why I feel your patch series are really unclean. I dislike
special cases, I try to avoid them as much as possible.

Chris

reviews.author: Rik Riel
reviews.summary: Rik Riel questioned whether a similar abstraction layer to VFS is needed for the swap side, suggesting that the filesystem layer's cleanliness is due to its existing VFS abstraction.
reviews.raw_body:
The filesystem layer is relatively clean because
it has a VFS.

Are you saying it is time we have a similar
abstraction layer on the swap side?

-- 
All Rights Reversed.

reviews.author: Chris Li
reviews.summary: Reviewer Chris Li noted that the patch's interface choice for swapon/swapoff does not make sense, as it exposes an interface with only one correct answer and lacks real userspace use cases to justify its design.
reviews.raw_body:
Yes, you understand me well. The swap side VFS already started as
swap_ops. I give a LSF/MM talk on it as well. It is already cleaning
up some ZRAM special cases in the block layer. That is what xswap is
building on top of.

Chris

2026-09-24.patch_summary: This patch adds infrastructure for virtual swap devices, which have specific requirements and behaviors that differ from physical swap devices. Without this special casing, undesirable problems can arise, such as incorrect allocation of swap slots and per-CPU caching issues. The patch addresses these problems by adding a check to ensure that the correct device is being used for each operation, allowing for more efficient and reliable use of virtual swap devices.
